title: UK Parliament Demands Probe as Pakistan's PoK Crackdown Kills Over 40 Civilians
excerpt: British MPs call for urgent diplomatic intervention as Amnesty International condemns lethal force against protesters in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.
body:
• Over 40 civilians killed and hundreds arrested in Pakistan's crackdown on protesters in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir since June 2026
  • British MPs demand urgent talks with Pakistan's High Commissioner and call for Foreign Office intervention
  • An estimated 50,000 British Kashmiris marched in London from Parliament Square to the Pakistan High Commission
  • Amnesty International calls for independent investigation and immediate lifting of communications blackout

British parliamentarians have demanded an independent investigation into what they called a "deeply alarming" crackdown by Pakistani security forces in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, where over 40 civilians have been killed and hundreds arrested since early June.

The All-Party Parliamentary Group on Kashmir, a cross-party body in the UK Parliament, has made two formal demands: urgent talks with Pakistan's High Commissioner in London, and meetings with Foreign Office ministers to ensure diplomatic representations are being made "at the highest level."

Mounting Death Toll and Communications Blackout

The crisis began in early June when Pakistani security forces opened fire on protesters in Rawalakot, triggering widespread unrest across PoK. The violence has since spread to multiple districts, with the lakeside town of Dadyal in Mirpur becoming a primary flashpoint.

According to testimony at the 62nd session of the United Nations Human Rights Council, more than 22 people had been killed, 576 arrested, and 34 booked under anti-terrorism laws by late June. By late July, the death toll had climbed past 40, according to IANS, with dozens more critically injured.

Pakistani authorities imposed a complete communications blackout, with internet services suspended for over 30 consecutive days. Roads connecting the region to Pakistan were blocked by police and Rangers, disrupting the movement of food, medicines, and other essential supplies.

"The restrictions could trigger widespread unrest across the region. This is cruelty rather than politics."

— Mirza Shafiq, Chairman, Swiss Kashmir Human Rights Commission

UK Lawmakers Sound the Alarm

Labour MP Liam Byrne described reports of live fire against peaceful protesters as "deeply alarming" and called the communications blackout "completely unacceptable." He urged both immediate de-escalation and adherence to long-standing UN resolutions on Kashmir.

MP Adnan Hussain called the killings a "tragedy" and demanded that any use of excessive or unlawful force be subject to "a full, independent and transparent investigation." He noted particular concern for constituents with family in the region.

50,000 March in London

The crisis has galvanized Britain's Kashmiri diaspora, one of the largest outside South Asia. An estimated 50,000 British Kashmiris participated in the London Kashmir Million March, walking from Parliament Square to the Pakistan High Commission to demand an end to the violence and the release of detained political activists, including Shaukat Nawaz Mir, head of the Joint Awami Action Committee.

The march drew solidarity from Baloch and Pashtun communities in the UK, who highlighted what they described as parallel human rights violations by Pakistan's military in their own regions.

International Pressure Builds

Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard said the reports from Rawalakot reflected Pakistan's long-standing pattern of "unlawful violence" against protesters. She called on Pakistani authorities to lift the communications blackout and allow media and independent observers access to the region.

The United Kashmir People's National Party staged a separate demonstration at the Broken Chair monument outside the UN headquarters in Geneva, timed to coincide with the UNHRC session. UKPNP leaders condemned the June 7 firing incident in Rawalakot and called for unrestricted access for international human rights organizations.

"So long as an internet and mobile services blackout remains in place, it will severely impede the independent verification of the full extent of the situation on the ground."

— Agnes Callamard, Secretary General, Amnesty International

What's Next

The crisis shows no signs of abating. The UKPNP and the Swiss Kashmir Human Rights Commission have submitted an urgent appeal to UN Secretary-General António Guterres and the UN Human Rights Council, demanding an independent fact-finding mission to investigate the alleged extrajudicial killings.

For Britain's estimated 1.2 million-strong Kashmiri diaspora — many of whom trace their roots to the heavily impacted Mirpur district — the crackdown has become a deeply personal crisis. UK parliamentary scrutiny is expected to intensify as the humanitarian situation deteriorates.
